title: Structural Patterns Compared and Combined
scopeHtml: Scope: Comparison tables, how to choose, combining patterns, end-to-end Adapter+Decorator+Facade example.

notes.title: The seven at a glance
notes.html:
Seven structural patterns, one line each. Learn them as a table; interviews ask you to pick.

Pattern One-line purpose Wraps Key phrase
Adapter Make A look like B one object "translate"
Bridge Separate two axes of change holds an implementor "A + B not A x B"
Composite Treat one and many uniformly many children "tree"
Decorator Add behavior at runtime one object, same interface "stackable layers"
Facade One easy door to a subsystem many objects "simplify"
Flyweight Share immutable state to save memory pool of shared parts "cache objects"
Proxy Control access to an object one object, same interface "gatekeeper"

Industry examples. Each appears in code you use daily: InputStreamReader (Adapter), JDBC (Bridge), ViewGroup (Composite), BufferedReader (Decorator), JdbcTemplate (Facade), Integer.valueOf (Flyweight), Retrofit services (Proxy).

Everyday analogy. A toolbox: each tool shapes a different kind of fix. Choosing the right one is the skill.

Common interview traps.

  • Reciting definitions instead of choosing based on a problem.
  • Trying to name a pattern for every class.

notes.title: Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy
notes.html:
These three all wrap ONE object, so they look alike in a UML diagram. The difference is intent and interface.

Interface vs wrapped Intent Typical question
Adapter DIFFERENT from the wrapped Make incompatible things fit "I have X, client wants Y"
Decorator SAME as the wrapped Add responsibilities "Add logging/compression/encryption"
Proxy SAME as the wrapped Control access / lifecycle "Delay, protect, remote, cache" 
Adapter   : Client -> [Target iface] AdapterImpl -> Adaptee (other iface)
Decorator : Client -> [Same iface]   Wrapper     -> Component (adds work)
Proxy     : Client -> [Same iface]   Proxy       -> RealSubject (gates it)

Worked example. Same class FileSource. (1) You need it to look like Reader: Adapter. (2) You want every read() timed and buffered: Decorator. (3) You want it opened only on first read and only for admins: Proxy. A decorator is usually built by the CALLER (new Buffered(src)); a proxy often creates or locates the real subject itself.

Industry examples. InputStreamReader is an Adapter; BufferedInputStream a Decorator; a Hibernate lazy entity a Proxy; Retrofit builds a Proxy, its CallAdapter is an Adapter, its OkHttp interceptors are a chain of decorators.

Everyday analogy. Adapter is a plug converter, Decorator is a phone case (still a phone, more features), Proxy is your assistant (answers for you, may refuse).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "same thing, different name". Give the intent test.
  • Calling a wrapper that checks permissions a Decorator; if it controls access, it is a Proxy.

notes.title: Composite vs Decorator vs Facade vs Flyweight
notes.html:
Four patterns that people mix because they all "hold other objects".

Holds Relationship Goal
Composite Many children of the same type Tree, recursive Uniform part-whole
Decorator One inner of the same type Chain Add behavior
Facade Several DIFFERENT subsystem classes Fan-out Simplify use
Flyweight A pool of shared parts Many users to few objects Save memory

Worked example. A UI toolkit uses all four: widgets form a Composite tree; a scrollbar is added with a Decorator (ScrollDecorator(textBox)); one Toolkit.show(dialog) call is a Facade over layout, theming and windowing; glyph shapes for each character are Flyweights (about 100 shared glyphs instead of 1,000,000 character objects).

Industry examples. Android: ViewGroup (Composite), ContextWrapper (Decorator), MediaPlayer (Facade), RecycledViewPool (Flyweight).

Everyday analogy. A company: org chart (Composite), job titles added to a person (Decorator), the reception desk (Facade), shared photocopier (Flyweight).

Common interview traps.

  • Facade holds DIFFERENT types; Composite holds the SAME type.
  • Flyweight is about memory, not about behavior.

notes.title: How to choose
notes.html:
Ask these questions in order. The first "yes" is usually the pattern.

  1. Interfaces do not match and you cannot change one side? Adapter.
  2. Two independent dimensions would multiply classes? Bridge.
  3. Part-whole tree you want to treat uniformly? Composite.
  4. Need to add optional behavior in layers at runtime? Decorator.
  5. Callers repeat a multi-step recipe over many classes? Facade.
  6. Millions of near-identical objects eating memory? Flyweight (after measuring).
  7. Need to delay, guard, remote or cache access? Proxy.
  8. Several cross-cutting steps in sequence for each request? Interceptor chain.

Decision gravity. Patterns are cheap to add and usually reversible, except where they are exposed in a public API (a Facade's methods, a Bridge's interface) or where order matters (interceptors). Start without a pattern; add one when the second concrete case or pain appears (rule of three).

Everyday analogy. Choosing a container: bag, box, or suitcase; pick after you know what you are carrying.

Common interview traps.

  • Introducing a pattern before a real problem exists (over-engineering).
  • Not naming the cost: each pattern adds classes, indirection and a place to debug.
  • Forgetting that language features may replace patterns (Kotlin by, lambdas, lazy).

notes.title: Combining patterns
notes.html:
Real systems layer patterns. Know the common pairs:

  • Composite + Decorator: decorate a node in a tree (add a border to any View, leaf or group).
  • Facade + Adapter: the facade uses adapters to talk to several vendor SDKs (payments, SMS, maps).
  • Proxy + Flyweight: a proxy returns shared instances.
  • Decorator chain = interceptor chain: OkHttp is exactly layered wrappers.
  • Bridge + Adapter: bridge the abstraction; adapt each third-party implementor.

Worked example. An Android repository: UserRepository (Facade) calls UserApi (Retrofit remote Proxy); OkHttp interceptors (Decorators) add auth and logging; a CallAdapter (Adapter) converts Call<User> to suspend; Room-backed cache is the Caching Proxy idea. Five patterns, none of them named in the code but all present.

Industry examples. Spring: AOP proxies plus decorator-like filters plus facades like JdbcTemplate. Retrofit/OkHttp as above.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant: host (Facade), menu board (Flyweight-like shared), waiter (Proxy to the kitchen), kitchen stations (Composite of cooks).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying you will use all seven. Mention the one or two that earn their place.
  • Not being able to point to the pattern in a library you use daily.

notes.title: End-to-end example: notification service
notes.html:
Requirement: send a notification to a user through SMS or email, using a vendor SDK that has a different API, with logging and rate-limiting, and a simple call for the app. We use three patterns: Adapter (vendor SDK), Decorator (logging and rate-limit), Facade (the app's single entry point).

+-----------------------+
| NotificationFacade    |  <- Facade: one method for the app
| + notify(user, text)  |
+----------+------------+
           | uses
           v
+----------+-----------+   <<Sender>>
| RateLimitingSender   |------------+  Decorator
+----------+-----------+            |
           | wraps                  |
+----------v-----------+            |
| LoggingSender        |------------+  Decorator
+----------+-----------+
           | wraps
+----------v-----------+      adapts      +----------------+
| TwilioAdapter        | ---------------> | TwilioSdk      |  Adapter
+----------------------+                  | sendSms(...)   |
                                          +----------------+
import java.util.*;

interface Sender { boolean send(String user, String text); }

class TwilioSdk {                                   // vendor: odd signature
    int sendSms(String e164, String body, boolean flash) { return 200; }
}

class TwilioAdapter implements Sender {             // ADAPTER
    private final TwilioSdk sdk;
    TwilioAdapter(TwilioSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    public boolean send(String user, String text) {
        return sdk.sendSms("+91" + user, text, false) == 200;
    }
}

class LoggingSender implements Sender {             // DECORATOR
    private final Sender inner;
    LoggingSender(Sender inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    public boolean send(String user, String text) {
        boolean ok = inner.send(user, text);
        System.out.println("send to " + user + " ok=" + ok);
        return ok;
    }
}

class RateLimitingSender implements Sender {        // DECORATOR
    private final Sender inner; private final int maxPerUser;
    private final Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
    RateLimitingSender(Sender inner, int max) { this.inner = inner; this.maxPerUser = max; }
    public boolean send(String user, String text) {
        int c = counts.merge(user, 1, Integer::sum);
        if (c > maxPerUser) return false;           // short-circuit
        return inner.send(user, text);
    }
}

class NotificationFacade {                          // FACADE
    private final Sender sender;
    NotificationFacade(Sender sender) { this.sender = sender; }
    public boolean notify(String user, String text) { return sender.send(user, text); }
}

public class Demo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Sender chain = new RateLimitingSender(new LoggingSender(new TwilioAdapter(new TwilioSdk())), 2);
        NotificationFacade facade = new NotificationFacade(chain);
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) System.out.println(facade.notify("9876543210", "hi " + i));
        // prints true, true, false (third blocked by the rate limiter, never logged)
    }
}
interface Sender { fun send(user: String, text: String): Boolean }

class TwilioAdapter(private val sdk: TwilioSdk) : Sender {                // Adapter
    override fun send(user: String, text: String) = sdk.sendSms("+91$user", text, false) == 200
}
class LoggingSender(private val inner: Sender) : Sender by inner {        // Decorator
    override fun send(user: String, text: String) =
        inner.send(user, text).also { println("send to $user ok=$it") }
}
class RateLimitingSender(private val inner: Sender, private val max: Int) : Sender by inner {
    private val counts = HashMap<String, Int>()
    override fun send(user: String, text: String): Boolean {
        val c = counts.merge(user, 1, Int::plus)!!
        return c <= max && inner.send(user, text)
    }
}
class NotificationFacade(private val sender: Sender) {                    // Facade
    fun notify(user: String, text: String) = sender.send(user, text)
}

Why this order. Rate limiting is outermost so blocked calls do not cost a vendor call or log noise. Logging sits close to the vendor to record real outcomes. Swapping Twilio for another vendor touches ONE class (the adapter). Adding metrics = one more decorator.

Concurrency note. The demo's HashMap counter is not thread-safe; in production use ConcurrentHashMap or Redis counters with a TTL (for example, 5 messages per user per minute) so limits hold across servers.

Common interview traps.

  • Placing rate limiting after the vendor call, which defeats it.
  • Naming the patterns but not explaining what each removes (vendor lock-in, repeated cross-cutting code, caller complexity).
  • Shared mutable state in a decorator without thread safety.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Seven structural patterns: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy; all use composition.
  • Adapter changes the interface; Decorator and Proxy keep it. Decorator adds behavior; Proxy controls access.
  • Composite holds many of the same type; Facade fronts many different types; Flyweight shares immutable parts to save memory.
  • Choose by the problem: mismatch, two axes, tree, layers, simplify, memory, access control, cross-cutting chain.
  • Patterns combine: a networking stack uses Facade over a Retrofit Proxy with OkHttp interceptors (decorators) and a CallAdapter (adapter).
  • End-to-end: Facade -> RateLimit/Logging decorators -> Adapter -> vendor SDK; order matters.
  • Add a pattern when a real pain appears; Kotlin by, lambdas and lazy often replace boilerplate.

questions.promptHtml: Adapter, Decorator and Proxy all wrap one object and look identical in a UML diagram. How do you tell them apart?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who recite definitions fail here. The signal is whether you test intent and interface, not shape.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I ask two questions. Does the wrapper expose a different interface from the wrapped object? Then it is an Adapter. Same interface: is it adding behavior (Decorator) or controlling access to the object (Proxy)? Shape is the same, intent differs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Adapter   : Client -> [Target iface] AdapterImpl -> Adaptee (other iface)
Decorator : Client -> [Same iface]   Wrapper     -> Component (adds work)
Proxy     : Client -> [Same iface]   Proxy       -> RealSubject (gates it)
  • Adapter: you own the client's interface, you cannot change the other side (vendor SDK, legacy class). It translates calls.
  • Decorator: the caller builds the stack (new Buffered(src)), each layer adds a responsibility, layers are stackable and reorderable.
  • Proxy: often creates or locates the real subject itself, and decides whether, when or where the call happens (lazy load, auth, remote, cache). Same class FileSource: look like Reader is an Adapter; time every read() is a Decorator; open only on first read and only for admins is a Proxy.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Reader { String read(); }
class FileSource { String load() { return "data"; } }          // other interface

class FileAdapter implements Reader {                          // Adapter: different interface
    private final FileSource src = new FileSource();
    public String read() { return src.load(); }
}
class TimedReader implements Reader {                          // Decorator: same iface, adds timing
    private final Reader in; TimedReader(Reader in) { this.in = in; }
    public String read() { long t = System.nanoTime(); String s = in.read(); System.out.println(System.nanoTime() - t); return s; }
}
class AdminOnlyReader implements Reader {                      // Proxy: same iface, gates access
    private final Reader in; private final boolean admin;
    AdminOnlyReader(Reader in, boolean admin) { this.in = in; this.admin = admin; }
    public String read() { if (!admin) throw new SecurityException(); return in.read(); }
}
interface Reader { fun read(): String }
class FileSource { fun load() = "data" }

class FileAdapter(private val src: FileSource = FileSource()) : Reader {      // Adapter
    override fun read() = src.load()
}
class TimedReader(private val inner: Reader) : Reader {                       // Decorator
    override fun read(): String { val t = System.nanoTime(); return inner.read().also { println(System.nanoTime() - t) } }
}
class AdminOnlyReader(private val inner: Reader, private val admin: Boolean) : Reader {  // Proxy
    override fun read() = if (admin) inner.read() else throw SecurityException()
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "same thing, different name" with no intent test.
  • Calling a permission-checking wrapper a Decorator. If it controls access, it is a Proxy.
  • Forgetting the Adapter changes the interface; Decorator and Proxy must not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Which one is BufferedInputStream? -> Decorator. InputStreamReader is an Adapter (bytes to chars).
  2. Where is the Proxy in Retrofit? -> Retrofit builds a dynamic proxy for your interface; its CallAdapter is an Adapter; OkHttp interceptors are decorator-like layers.
  3. A wrapper that adds caching: Decorator or Proxy? -> If it is cross-cutting behavior stacked by the caller, Decorator; if it controls whether the real call happens, Caching Proxy. Both are defensible; name your intent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists three definitions. The senior gives the interface-and-intent test and points to each in a library they use daily.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team named a security wrapper "Decorator", then someone stacked it below a cache; cached results were served without the permission check. Calling it a Proxy made the ordering rule obvious.

questions.promptHtml: Composite, Decorator, Facade and Flyweight all "hold other objects". What does each hold and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you see the shape of the relationship (tree, chain, fan-out, pool) and the goal behind it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Composite holds many children of the SAME type in a tree, so one and many are treated uniformly. Decorator holds ONE inner of the same type in a chain to add behavior. Facade holds several DIFFERENT subsystem classes to simplify use. Flyweight is a pool of shared immutable parts to save memory.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Holds Relationship Goal
Composite Many same-type children Tree, recursive Uniform part-whole
Decorator One same-type inner Chain Add behavior
Facade Several different classes Fan-out Simplify
Flyweight Pool of shared parts Many users, few objects Memory 
Composite: Group -> [Leaf, Group -> [Leaf, Leaf]]     same type, recursive
Facade   : Facade -> Layout, Theme, Window            different types

A UI toolkit uses all four: widgets form a Composite tree; a scrollbar is a Decorator; Toolkit.show(dialog) is a Facade; glyph shapes are Flyweights (about 100 shared glyphs instead of 1,000,000 character objects).

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Facade holds DIFFERENT types; Composite holds the SAME type.
  • Flyweight is about memory, not behavior.
  • Making a Facade the only way in, so power users cannot reach the subsystem.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Android example of each? -> ViewGroup (Composite), ContextWrapper (Decorator), MediaPlayer (Facade), RecycledViewPool (Flyweight).
  2. Can Composite and Decorator combine? -> Yes: a border decorator on any View, leaf or group.
  3. Why must Flyweight state be immutable and intrinsic? -> Shared objects are used by many owners; per-owner (extrinsic) state must be passed in by the caller or sharing corrupts it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "they all wrap things". Senior: names the fan shape, the goal, and the pitfall (Facade bloat, mutable flyweight).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "ServiceFacade" grew 60 methods and became a god class; splitting by use case restored its purpose.

questions.contextHtml: Four small requirements land in one sprint. (a) Your code expects PaymentGateway.pay(amount), but a new vendor SDK offers Client.charge(cents, currency, metadata). (b) A file explorer shows folders containing files and other folders; "total size" must work on either. (c) The app calls five classes in a fixed order to place an order, and three screens duplicate that recipe. (d) You must add optional encryption and compression to a byte stream, in any combination.
questions.promptHtml: Pick a pattern for each and justify it in one line.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use Factory everywhere" or naming the right patterns without the reason, then proposing all of them for (a) as well.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I change the vendor SDK? (no). Is the tree depth fixed? (no, so recursion). Is the order recipe stable? Which combinations of (d) are needed at runtime?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I go through the "how to choose" order and stop at the first yes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) interfaces mismatch and I cannot change one side: Adapter. (b) part-whole tree: Composite, size() on a common interface. (c) callers repeat a multi-step recipe over many classes: Facade OrderService.place(...). (d) optional layers in any combination: Decorator (new Encrypting(new Compressing(out))).
  4. How I'd verify each: Draw the call: does a wrapper change the interface (Adapter) or keep it (Decorator)? Count combinations: 2 options give 4 combos, which would be 4 subclasses without Decorator.
  5. Root cause: Not a bug; the point is matching a named pain to a pattern.
  6. Fix: Implement the smallest version of each; for (a) one class translating pay to charge.
  7. Prevention: In review ask "which pain does this pattern remove?" If nobody can answer, remove it.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a Bridge or Flyweight; nothing here has two axes or memory pressure.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Two vendors with different SDKs appear in (a)? -> One Adapter per vendor behind the same interface, picked by config.
  • (c) callers now need to skip step 3? -> Facade stays for the common path; subsystem remains accessible.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A new hire wrapped every class in a Decorator "for flexibility"; stack traces grew five frames and nobody could find where a header was added. We kept patterns only where a second case existed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names patterns by guess, no reasons.
  • Hire: all four correct with a one-line reason each.
  • Strong hire: also states what is NOT needed and the rule of three.

questions.contextHtml:
Support reports: after a release, the vendor bill for SMS went up 40% and a user with a limit of 2 messages per day got 6. The wiring was changed in a refactor.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
Sender chain = new LoggingSender(
                   new TwilioAdapter(
                       new RateLimitingSender(new RealSdkSender(), 2)));
// RateLimitingSender now wraps the vendor SDK call; Adapter and Logging sit above it
NotificationFacade facade = new NotificationFacade(chain);
val chain = LoggingSender(TwilioAdapter(RateLimitingSender(RealSdkSender(), 2)))

Logs show "send to 9876543210 ok=false" for blocked calls, and the vendor dashboard shows retries by the app's caller.
questions.promptHtml: Find the problems in this wiring and fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the limit" or "add a cache", missing that order of decorators changes what the limiter counts and what is logged.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the caller retry on false? Is the counter per process or shared? What did the chain look like before the refactor?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert to the previous wiring; set a vendor-side spend cap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) limiter is below the adapter so it counts raw SDK calls but a retrying caller multiplies them; (2) per-process counter, with N pods the effective limit is N x 2; (3) Logging outermost records blocked calls as noise and hides real vendor outcomes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare vendor call count with limiter count per user; check pod count; grep logs for blocked entries.
  5. Root cause: Ordering. The correct chain is RateLimit -> Logging -> Adapter -> SDK: blocked calls short-circuit before they cost a vendor call or a log line, and logging sits near the vendor to record real outcomes.
  6. Fix: new RateLimitingSender(new LoggingSender(new TwilioAdapter(sdk)), 2). Long-term: Redis counter with TTL so the limit holds across servers.
  7. Prevention: One test: send 3, assert vendor fake called twice. Build chains in one factory method, not scattered.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make the limiter a Proxy to "fix" it; it is the same chain either way, ordering is the lesson.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Should blocked sends be logged? -> Yes, but at a separate metric or a log layer ABOVE the limiter, not mixed with vendor outcomes.
  • Caller retries on false: bug? -> Return a distinct result (RATE_LIMITED vs FAILED) so callers do not retry a block.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A refactor moved retry above a limiter; a 30 second vendor blip turned 1 message into 5, and the cap protected nothing.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: changes limits only.
  • Hire: restores correct order and explains short-circuit.
  • Strong hire: also fixes distributed counting and result typing.

questions.contextHtml:
CheckoutService is 900 lines. It imports a card SDK, a UPI SDK and an SMS SDK, calls them directly, and has if (method.equals("UPI")) branches in 14 places. Product wants a third payment method next month, and unit tests need real sandbox keys.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class CheckoutService {
    boolean pay(String method, long paise, String user) {
        if (method.equals("CARD")) { CardSdk c = new CardSdk(KEY); return c.authorize(paise / 100.0, "INR").ok; }
        else if (method.equals("UPI")) { return new UpiSdk().collect(user + "@upi", (int) paise).status == 1; }
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(method);
    }
}
class CheckoutService {
    fun pay(method: String, paise: Long, user: String): Boolean = when (method) {
        "CARD" -> CardSdk(KEY).authorize(paise / 100.0, "INR").ok
        "UPI" -> UpiSdk().collect("$user@upi", paise.toInt()).status == 1
        else -> throw IllegalArgumentException(method)
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: Refactor: which classes appear and which patterns do they represent?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make it a Strategy" without noticing the SDK APIs differ (that is an adaptation problem) and without a single entry point for callers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can I change SDKs? (no). Do all methods return a bool or do we need codes? Is the amount in paise everywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin behavior with characterization tests before moving code.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Pain 1: SDK mismatch, so Adapter per SDK behind PaymentGateway. Pain 2: callers know the recipe, so Facade CheckoutFacade.pay(...) picks the gateway. Pain 3: a registry keyed by method replaces the if-chain.
  4. How I'd verify each: Tests with a fake PaymentGateway; grep that no import of SDKs remains outside adapters.
  5. Root cause: One class knows three vendors and one selection rule; every change touches it (violates open/closed).
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(long paise, String user); }
class CardAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final CardSdk sdk; CardAdapter(CardSdk s) { sdk = s; }
    public boolean pay(long paise, String user) { return sdk.authorize(paise / 100.0, "INR").ok; }
}
class CheckoutFacade {
    private final Map<String, PaymentGateway> byMethod;
    CheckoutFacade(Map<String, PaymentGateway> m) { byMethod = m; }
    boolean pay(String method, long paise, String user) {
        PaymentGateway g = byMethod.get(method);
        if (g == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(method);
        return g.pay(paise, user);
    }
}
interface PaymentGateway { fun pay(paise: Long, user: String): Boolean }
class CardAdapter(private val sdk: CardSdk) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(paise: Long, user: String) = sdk.authorize(paise / 100.0, "INR").ok
}
class CheckoutFacade(private val byMethod: Map<String, PaymentGateway>) {
    fun pay(method: String, paise: Long, user: String) =
        (byMethod[method] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException(method)).pay(paise, user)
}
  1. Prevention: Adapter tests with the SDK stubbed; adding a method = one new adapter plus one map entry.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not add a Bridge unless payment methods also vary on a second axis (for example region). I would not hide the gateways from callers that legitimately need one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Third method needs 2-step auth? -> Its adapter hides the two steps; the interface stays pay, or widen it if every method needs it.
  • Facade has grown to 40 methods? -> Split by use case (CheckoutFacade, RefundFacade).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: After this split, adding a wallet took half a day and one reviewer; before it, it touched 14 branches and broke UPI twice.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only extract methods.
  • Hire: Adapter + Facade with registry.
  • Strong hire: explains why not Bridge, and how tests become trivial.

questions.contextHtml: The notification chain is NotificationFacade -> RateLimit -> Logging -> TwilioAdapter -> TwilioSdk. Product now wants: (1) email as a second channel using a different vendor SDK; (2) metrics (success and latency per channel); (3) fall back to email if SMS fails.
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change, which are added, and where does each new piece sit in the chain?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Edit TwilioAdapter to also send email, or add if (channel == EMAIL) to the Facade, breaking open/closed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the fallback automatic or user-chosen? Should the rate limit be per channel or per user overall? Is a duplicate message (both arrive) acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I keep the existing chain working while adding new classes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) Email = new EmailAdapter implements Sender; zero edits to existing classes. (2) Metrics = a new MetricsSender decorator; near Logging, inside the limiter. (3) Fallback = a FallbackSender(primary, secondary) decorator-like class that tries the secondary when the primary returns false.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fakes for both senders: primary false, assert secondary called once; limiter still blocks first.
  5. Root cause: Not a bug: the design absorbs the change because each concern is one class behind Sender.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class FallbackSender implements Sender {
    private final Sender primary, secondary;
    FallbackSender(Sender p, Sender s) { primary = p; secondary = s; }
    public boolean send(String user, String text) { return primary.send(user, text) || secondary.send(user, text); }
}
Sender sms   = new MetricsSender(new LoggingSender(new TwilioAdapter(twilio)), "sms");
Sender email = new MetricsSender(new LoggingSender(new EmailAdapter(mail)), "email");
Sender chain = new RateLimitingSender(new FallbackSender(sms, email), 2);
class FallbackSender(private val primary: Sender, private val secondary: Sender) : Sender {
    override fun send(user: String, text: String) = primary.send(user, text) || secondary.send(user, text)
}
val sms = MetricsSender(LoggingSender(TwilioAdapter(twilio)), "sms")
val email = MetricsSender(LoggingSender(EmailAdapter(mail)), "email")
val chain = RateLimitingSender(FallbackSender(sms, email), 2)
  1. Prevention: A wiring test for the chain order; metrics tagged by channel.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: The limiter wraps the fallback so one logical notification counts once; putting it per channel would let a fallback double count. I would not put channel ifs in the Facade.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Primary timed out but actually delivered? -> Fallback duplicates; use an idempotency key or accept at-least-once and say so.
  • Which existing classes changed? -> None, only the composition root (the wiring).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team added push notifications the same way in one day; the only edited file was the factory that builds the chain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits existing classes.
  • Hire: new adapter plus decorators, correct placement.
  • Strong hire: raises idempotency and limiter placement relative to fallback.

questions.promptHtml: When do you introduce a structural pattern, and when do you deliberately not?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Seniors are judged by restraint. Candidates who add a pattern per class create indirection nobody can debug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start without a pattern and add one when a real pain shows up, usually the second or third concrete case (rule of three). I name the pain first: mismatch, two axes, tree, layers, simplify, memory, access. If I cannot name it, I do not add the pattern, because each one adds classes, indirection and a place to debug.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Decision order from the notes: mismatch (Adapter), two axes (Bridge), tree (Composite), optional layers (Decorator), repeated recipe (Facade), millions of near-identical objects after measuring (Flyweight), delay/guard/remote/cache (Proxy), ordered cross-cutting steps (interceptor chain). Decision gravity: patterns are cheap and reversible, except where exposed in a public API (a Facade's methods, a Bridge's interface) or where order matters (interceptors). Those are one-way doors: callers depend on them.

1 case  -> write it directly
2 cases -> tolerate duplication, note it
3 cases -> now the shape is visible: extract the pattern

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Introducing a pattern before a real problem (over-engineering).
  • Not naming the cost: classes, indirection, harder stack traces.
  • Forgetting language features: Kotlin by, lambdas and lazy replace boilerplate.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Example where a lambda replaces a pattern? -> A one-method decorator or strategy becomes a function (Request) -> Response.
  2. Which patterns are hardest to undo? -> Public Facades and Bridge interfaces, and interceptor order.
  3. How do you review for over-engineering? -> Ask "which pain does this remove today?" and count callers of each new interface.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: lists all seven. Senior: names one or two that earn their place, the cost, and the reversibility.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A service had UserFacadeImpl over UserServiceImpl over UserManager, each forwarding calls; onboarding took a week to find where logic lived.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin's by keyword generates a decorator for you. What are its limits and gotchas?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks if you understand what delegation really generates and where self-calls bypass the wrapper.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: class A(inner: I) : I by inner generates forwarding methods for every interface member, so I override only what I change. The gotcha: calls made inside the inner object to its own other methods do NOT go through my wrapper, and delegation works only for interfaces, not classes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Java needs hand-written forwarders for every method; adding a method to the interface breaks every decorator at compile time (or silently forwards in Kotlin). Kotlin forwards automatically.

The self-call problem:

Wrapper.sendAll(list) -> inner.sendAll(list)
                              inner.sendAll calls this.send(x)   // inner's own send,
                              not Wrapper.send -> wrapper logic skipped
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Sender { boolean send(String u, String t); boolean sendAll(List<String> users, String t); }
class Base implements Sender {
    public boolean send(String u, String t) { return true; }
    public boolean sendAll(List<String> users, String t) {
        users.forEach(u -> send(u, t));          // calls Base.send, bypasses any wrapper
        return true;
    }
}
class Limited(private val inner: Sender) : Sender by inner {
    override fun send(u: String, t: String) = if (allowed(u)) inner.send(u, t) else false
}
// Limited.sendAll is forwarded to inner.sendAll, which calls Base.send: the limit is skipped

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming the wrapper intercepts every call; self-calls inside inner skip it.
  • Delegating a concrete class (not allowed; only interfaces).
  • Forgetting new interface methods get forwarded silently with no limit logic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you fix the self-call bypass? -> Override sendAll in the wrapper too, or make sendAll loop over this.send in a shared default method of the interface.
  2. Java equivalent trick? -> Dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) or a base ForwardingX class (Guava-style).
  3. Does AOP have the same problem? -> Yes: Spring proxy-based AOP does not intercept self-invocation inside the target.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "by saves boilerplate". Senior: names the self-call bypass and the silent-forward risk when the interface grows.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rate limit added as a Spring proxy was skipped for batch calls routed through the same bean's internal method; the cap silently never applied to batch sends.

questions.contextHtml: A map-rendering service keeps 2,000,000 Marker objects in memory. Each stores x, y, a 64x64 icon as byte[16384], a String name and a Color. Heap use is 36 GB across the fleet, GC pauses reach 900 ms. There are only 40 distinct icons.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and what do you check before and after?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM" or "use a cache", or applying Flyweight blindly without measuring and without making shared state immutable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are icons ever mutated per marker? Do markers differ only by position? What is the p99 latency target?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Tune heap and GC to buy time; do not rewrite under pressure.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) icon bytes dominate: 2M x 16 KB is about 32 GB, matching the heap; (2) names duplicated; (3) object headers and boxed fields are minor.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap histogram (jmap -histo) or a profiler: byte[] share. Count distinct icons: 40.
  5. Root cause: Intrinsic (shared, immutable) state, the icon, is duplicated per marker, while only extrinsic state (x, y) differs.
  6. Fix: Flyweight: IconFactory returns one of 40 shared immutable Icon objects; Marker keeps x, y and a reference. Memory: 40 x 16 KB = 640 KB plus 2M x about 24 bytes = about 48 MB.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
final class Icon { final byte[] pixels; Icon(byte[] p) { pixels = p; } }
class IconFactory {
    private static final Map<String, Icon> POOL = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static Icon get(String key) { return POOL.computeIfAbsent(key, IconFactory::load); }
}
record Marker(int x, int y, Icon icon) {}
class Icon(val pixels: ByteArray)
object IconFactory {
    private val pool = java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap<String, Icon>()
    fun get(key: String) = pool.computeIfAbsent(key) { load(it) }
}
data class Marker(val x: Int, val y: Int, val icon: Icon)
  1. Prevention: Memory budget test, alert on heap histogram share of byte[].
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use Flyweight before measuring; here the numbers justify it. Icon must be immutable, or one marker's edit changes all.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Users can recolor one marker's icon? -> That is extrinsic: store the tint on the marker, never mutate the shared icon.
  • Icons loaded forever? -> A pool with bounded size or weak references if the set is unbounded.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team "optimized" by pooling objects that were 40 bytes and had no duplication; the pool added lock contention and saved nothing. Measure first.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: more RAM.
  • Hire: Flyweight with intrinsic/extrinsic split and numbers.
  • Strong hire: immutability, bounded pool, and measure-first discipline.

questions.contextHtml:
The notification service now runs on 6 pods with 32 request threads each. The rate-limit decorator is the one from the demo: a HashMap<String,Integer> counter, limit 5 per user per minute. Symptoms: occasional ConcurrentModificationException and an infinite loop in HashMap.get pinning 2 cores (a known failure mode of unsynchronized HashMap in older JVMs; verify for your version); a user still got 22 messages in one minute; counts never reset.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
private final Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
public boolean send(String user, String text) {
    int c = counts.merge(user, 1, Integer::sum);
    if (c > maxPerUser) return false;
    return inner.send(user, text);
}
private val counts = HashMap<String, Int>()
override fun send(user: String, text: String): Boolean {
    val c = counts.merge(user, 1, Int::plus)!!
    return c <= max && inner.send(user, text)
}
questions.promptHtml: Explain every symptom and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make send synchronized", which serializes every send including the slow vendor call and still gives a per-pod limit.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the limit global or per pod? Fixed window or sliding? Is over-limit by a few acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap vendor spend; temporarily scale to 1 pod only if the cap is legally critical.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) shared HashMap with no synchronization: lost updates and corruption; (2) per-pod counters: 6 pods x 5 = up to 30 allowed; (3) no window reset: counts only grow, so users eventually blocked forever (the symptom "never reset").
  4. How I'd verify each: Thread dump showing threads stuck in HashMap; compare per-pod counters; a test with 32 threads and a fake sender.
  5. Root cause: Unsafe shared mutable state in a decorator plus a local counter for a global limit plus no expiry.
  6. Fix: Short-term: ConcurrentHashMap and merge (atomic per key). Real fix: shared store counter with TTL.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
// Redis fixed window: INCR key, set EXPIRE on first increment (verify atomic via a Lua script or INCR+EXPIRE pipeline)
long c = redis.incr("rl:" + user + ":" + (now / 60_000));
if (c == 1) redis.expire("rl:" + user + ":" + (now / 60_000), 60);
return c <= maxPerUser && inner.send(user, text);
val key = "rl:$user:${now / 60_000}"
val c = redis.incr(key)
if (c == 1L) redis.expire(key, 60)
return c <= max && inner.send(user, text)
  1. Prevention: Concurrency test; code review rule "no mutable instance fields in a decorator without a thread-safety note".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: synchronized on the whole method blocks vendor I/O. Redis failure: decide fail-open or fail-closed (usually fail-open with a local fallback for notifications; fail-closed for payments).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Fixed window lets 5 at 0:59 and 5 at 1:01? -> Yes, up to 2x burst; use sliding window or token bucket if that matters.
  • Redis is down? -> Fail-open with a small local limiter and alert.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A limiter on one pod "worked" in staging; in production with 6 pods users received 6x the cap and the vendor invoice showed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: synchronized method only.
  • Hire: ConcurrentHashMap plus shared store idea.
  • Strong hire: explains each symptom, window semantics and failure mode.

questions.contextHtml: QA asks how you will test the notification chain without calling Twilio and without sleeping for a real minute. Today TwilioAdapter does new TwilioSdk(System.getenv("KEY")) inside its constructor and RateLimitingSender calls System.currentTimeMillis().
questions.promptHtml: What do you change and what tests do you write for each layer?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a sandbox account", slow and flaky, or only integration tests of the whole chain.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the vendor SDK a class or an interface? Can I inject a clock? Which behaviors matter most (order, limit, mapping)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I refactor constructors first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Each layer is testable alone if its collaborator is injected: Adapter gets the SDK (or a thin interface over it), decorators get a fake Sender, the limiter gets a Clock.
  4. How I'd verify each: Per layer: Adapter maps "9876543210" to "+919876543210" and 200 to true (fake SDK records arguments); Logging calls inner once and returns its result; RateLimit with a fake Sender counting calls: three sends, inner called twice, third returns false, inner never called; advance the fake clock 61 s, send passes. Facade: one test that the chain order is correct (wiring test).
  5. Root cause: new inside constructors and static time calls hide dependencies.
  6. Fix:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface Clock { long now(); }
class FakeSender implements Sender {
    int calls; boolean result = true;
    public boolean send(String u, String t) { calls++; return result; }
}
// test
FakeSender fake = new FakeSender();
Sender limited = new RateLimitingSender(fake, 2, clock);
assertTrue(limited.send("u", "a")); assertTrue(limited.send("u", "b")); assertFalse(limited.send("u", "c"));
assertEquals(2, fake.calls);
class FakeSender(var result: Boolean = true) : Sender {
    var calls = 0
    override fun send(user: String, text: String): Boolean { calls++; return result }
}
val fake = FakeSender()
val limited = RateLimitingSender(fake, 2, clock)
check(limited.send("u", "a") && limited.send("u", "b") && !limited.send("u", "c"))
check(fake.calls == 2)
  1. Prevention: Composition root builds the chain; tests build their own; a single wiring test guards order.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mock with deep mock frameworks where a 5-line fake is clearer; I would not assert on log output text.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The SDK is a final class? -> Wrap in a thin interface (an Adapter itself), or use a mock maker that supports final; prefer the interface.
  • How to test failure of inner? -> Fake returns false or throws; assert the decorator's documented behavior.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Tests with a real Thread.sleep(61000) made CI take 40 minutes; an injected clock brought it to 2 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: sandbox only.
  • Hire: DI, fakes, per-layer tests.
  • Strong hire: clock injection, wiring test, fake over mock.

questions.contextHtml:
You review this PR adding caching and retry to a UserApi used by a repository. The wrapper stack is Repository (Facade) -> RetryApi -> CachingApi -> RetrofitApi.

Languages: Java · Kotlin
class CachingApi implements UserApi {
    private final UserApi inner; private final Map<String, User> cache = new HashMap<>();
    public User get(String id) { return cache.computeIfAbsent(id, inner::get); }
    public void update(User u) { inner.update(u); }           // cache not touched
}
class RetryApi implements UserApi {
    private final UserApi inner;
    public User get(String id) { return retry(3, () -> inner.get(id)); }
    public void update(User u) { retry(3, () -> { inner.update(u); return null; }); }
}
class CachingApi(private val inner: UserApi) : UserApi {
    private val cache = HashMap<String, User>()
    override fun get(id: String) = cache.getOrPut(id) { inner.get(id) }
    override fun update(u: User) = inner.update(u)             // cache not touched
}
class RetryApi(private val inner: UserApi) : UserApi {
    override fun get(id: String) = retry(3) { inner.get(id) }
    override fun update(u: User) = retry(3) { inner.update(u) }
}
questions.promptHtml: List what is wrong and say what you would request in the review.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Looks fine, nice use of decorators", or only nitpicks about naming.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is update idempotent (does the server dedupe)? How many threads share CachingApi? What staleness is acceptable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge; at minimum disable retry on update.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (1) update never invalidates the cache: stale reads after writes; (2) retry on a non-idempotent update can apply a change or charge twice if the first response was lost; (3) HashMap is not thread-safe and computeIfAbsent with a slow remote call; (4) cache never expires or bounds size; (5) retry wraps cache so a cached hit never retries (fine), but a failed get is not cached; order is right for reads, but needs thought for writes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test: get(1), update(1), get(1) must return new data. Test: fake inner throws timeout after applying; count applies. A thread test with 20 threads.
  5. Root cause: Cross-cutting layers added without defining read/write semantics, idempotency and thread safety.
  6. Fix: Invalidate on update (cache.remove(u.id()) after success); retry only get or send an idempotency key with update; ConcurrentHashMap plus TTL and max size (or Caffeine, verify availability in the project); keep the Facade as the only caller.
  7. Prevention: Review checklist for wrappers: interface behavior preserved, idempotency, thread safety, bounds, ordering test.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cache inside the retry layer or retry inside the cache loader without bounds; retrying a slow call under a map lock blocks other keys.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is this a Proxy or a Decorator? -> Caching that decides whether the real call happens is a Caching Proxy; retry adds behavior, a Decorator. Both keep the UserApi interface.
  • Multiple app instances? -> Local cache goes stale across instances: use TTL, a shared cache or events.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A profile screen showed old names after edits for 10 minutes because only get was cached and update bypassed the cache; separately, a retried POST created duplicate orders until an idempotency key was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves or nitpicks naming.
  • Hire: finds stale cache and non-idempotent retry.
  • Strong hire: also thread safety, bounds, order reasoning and idempotency keys.
